def: Combining form meaning fallopian tube, as in salpingitis (tube infection) and salpingo-oophoritis (tube and ovary), often from gonorrhea or chlamydia in pelvic inflammatory disease.
Relating to varices, abnormally dilated veins. Esophageal variceal bleeding is a major complication of portal hypertension in cirrhosis.
Describing metaplasia, a reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another that is better suited to a stress, such as Barrett esophagus or squamous change in smokers' bronchi.
Abnormally increased glomerular filtration rate in remaining or early-diabetic nephrons from dilated afferent arterioles. Over time it damages glomeruli and causes proteinuria.
Presence of abnormal glandular tissue, such as columnar epithelium in the vagina (vaginal adenosis) after in utero DES exposure, a precursor of clear cell carcinoma.
Affecting force of cardiac muscle contraction. Positive inotropes (digoxin, dobutamine) strengthen it; negative ones (beta blockers) weaken it.
Located behind the sternum, as in typical chest pain of myocardial infarction or esophageal conditions.
Abnormal over-expansion of the lungs from air trapping, as in emphysema, giving a barrel chest and flattened diaphragm on x-ray.
Surrounding the kidney tubules; peritubular capillaries return reabsorbed fluid to the blood and peritubular interstitial cells make erythropoietin.
Lung tissue filled with inflammatory exudate instead of air, as in lobar pneumonia. Produces dullness to percussion, bronchial breath sounds and an air-bronchogram on imaging.
An oral direct factor Xa inhibitor anticoagulant used for atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism. Reversed with andexanet alfa.
High solute concentration of plasma, as in uncontrolled hyperglycemia, which pulls water out of cells and causes dehydration and altered mental status.
Raising pH. Urease-producing bacteria alkalinize urine and promote struvite stones; sodium bicarbonate alkalinizes urine to speed excretion of salicylates.
An acetylcholinesterase reactivator used with atropine for organophosphate poisoning; it must be given early before the enzyme-inhibitor bond ages.
The caudate nucleus and putamen of the basal ganglia, which receive input from the cortex. Degeneration of striatal neurons causes Huntington disease.
Describing fungi that grow as molds at room temperature and as yeasts at body temperature, such as Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides and Sporothrix.
Fragmented, helmet-shaped red cells seen on blood smear in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia from DIC, TTP, HUS or HELLP syndrome, and mechanical heart valves.
Having had two or more prior deliveries beyond the age of viability.
A transfer RNA carrying its amino acid, made by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase using ATP, which proofreads the match. Enters the ribosomal A site.
Cell death in which tissue architecture is preserved for days with cell outlines intact, typical of ischemic infarcts in solid organs (not brain).
Preferentially acting on beta-1 receptors of the heart, as with metoprolol and atenolol, causing less bronchospasm than nonselective beta blockers.
The embryonic upper gut tube giving rise to the esophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, gallbladder and pancreas, supplied by the celiac artery.
Beneath the epithelium. Subepithelial immune deposits on glomerular basement membrane characterize membranous nephropathy.
Allowing x-rays to pass, so it looks dark on film. Uric acid stones are radiolucent, whereas calcium stones are radiopaque.
An area of skin supplied by sensory fibers of a single spinal nerve root, e.g., T4 at the nipple and T10 at the umbilicus. Shingles follows one.
Describing neutrophils with six or more nuclear lobes, a sign of megaloblastic anemia from B12 or folate deficiency.
Descending fibers from the hypothalamus to sympathetic neurons of the spinal cord. Interruption causes ipsilateral Horner syndrome.
Near the midline. The paramedian pontine reticular formation coordinates horizontal gaze; lesions cause ipsilateral gaze palsy.
Within the substance of an organ. Intraparenchymal brain hemorrhage is bleeding into brain tissue, usually from hypertension.
The smooth muscle layer of the gut wall (muscularis externa) or the thin muscle layer of the mucosa (muscularis mucosae).
Flat, small (under 1 cm) skin spots of altered color, like freckles or the lesions of tuberous sclerosis.
A recombinant PEGylated uricase that converts uric acid to allantoin, used for refractory chronic gout. Can cause infusion reactions; avoid in G6PD deficiency.
Large enveloped double-stranded DNA virus that unusually replicates in the cytoplasm. Includes variola (smallpox), vaccinia, and molluscum contagiosum.
Group D, catalase-negative gram-positive cocci in chains, normal gut flora, that cause UTI and endocarditis and are intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins; vancomycin-resistant strains are VRE.
Side and base of an epithelial cell facing the blood rather than the lumen, where the Na+/K+-ATPase usually sits.
Liver production of ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate) from acetyl-CoA during fasting, diabetic ketoacidosis or prolonged exercise.
Located within the wall of an organ, such as intramural uterine fibroids.
Drugs such as norepinephrine, vasopressin and phenylephrine that constrict blood vessels to raise blood pressure in shock.
